items.title: Who are you designing for?
items.description: "Everyone" is not a user. Pick a specific person, work out what they're trying to do, and design for them.

metadata.seoTitle: Who are you designing for? Defining your user
metadata.seoDescription: "Everyone" is not a user. Learn how to pick a specific person to design for, spot the people around them, and list the assumptions to test.

quiz.question: Which description is the better design target?
options: A first-year hosteller who studies at night on slow Wi-Fi
quiz.why: A specific situation tells you what to design. Broad groups don't.

quiz.question: What's the difference between a user and a buyer?
options: The user uses it, the buyer pays or decides, and they can be different people
quiz.why: Knowing who decides and who uses helps you design for both.

quiz.question: Why design for edge-case users?
options: Their problems often reveal issues that affect many people
quiz.why: One-handed use or slow internet isn't rare for long. Fixing it helps everyone.

quiz.question: What should you do with your assumptions?
options: Write them down and test the riskiest first
quiz.why: Naming a guess is the first step to checking it.

items.title: User interviews
items.description: A good interview is mostly listening. Ask about real moments from the past, not opinions about the future.

metadata.youllNeed: A friend to talk to; notes app or paper.
metadata.seoTitle: User interviews for beginners: how to ask and listen
metadata.seoDescription: Learn how to run your first user interview: ask about the last time, avoid leading questions, listen, and find patterns across a few conversations.

quiz.question: Which is the best interview question?
options: Would you use an app for this?
Tell me about the last time you booked a cab.
Don't you think booking cabs is hard?
quiz.why: It asks about a real past moment and doesn't suggest an answer.

quiz.question: Why is "Would you use my app?" a weak question?
options: People are polite and bad at predicting their own behavior
quiz.why: A polite "yes" tells you little about what they'd actually do.

quiz.question: There's a silence after someone answers. What do you do?
quiz.why: Silence often invites people to say something more honest.

quiz.question: Three of four people describe the same workaround. What is it?
quiz.why: Repetition is a signal, although a small group doesn't prove it for everyone.

items.title: Surveys that don't lie
items.description: Surveys tell you what and how many. Interviews tell you why. Write questions that don't push people toward an answer.

metadata.seoTitle: How to write a survey that gives honest answers
metadata.seoDescription: Surveys can tell you what and how many, but bad questions quietly lie. Learn the four ways questions go wrong and how to read results honestly.

quiz.question: Which question is leading?
options: How was your experience with checkout?
What did you use checkout for?
How many times did you use checkout?
quiz.why: It assumes the checkout was great, nudging the answer.

quiz.question: "Is the app fast and easy to use?" is a problem because...
options: It asks two things at once
quiz.why: A person might think it's fast but not easy. One question can't capture both.

quiz.question: What do surveys do better than interviews?
options: Show how many people said or did something
quiz.why: Surveys give counts. Interviews give reasons.

quiz.question: You get 12 responses. What's an honest way to report them?
quiz.why: Report counts and keep your claims modest.

items.title: Personas (without the cringe)
items.description: A persona is a short, honest summary of a real pattern you found in research. If it didn't come from real people, it's fiction.

metadata.seoTitle: Personas that actually help: a no-cringe guide
metadata.seoDescription: Most personas are fiction with stock photos. Learn how to build a short, honest persona from real research and actually use it in design decisions.

quiz.question: A useful persona is based on...
quiz.why: Research is what makes it trustworthy.

quiz.question: Which detail is the most useful to include?
options: Screenshots notes because he can't find them again
quiz.why: Behavior and frustration shape design decisions. Hobbies usually don't.

quiz.question: How many personas should you start with?
quiz.why: A few clear personas get used. A big pile gets ignored.

quiz.question: What does the "so we should..." line do?
options: Connects the pattern to a design decision
quiz.why: It turns a description into something you can act on.

items.title: Empathy maps
items.description: An empathy map is a one-page snapshot of what someone says, thinks, does and feels, so you can spot the gaps between them.

metadata.seoTitle: Empathy maps: see what users say, think, do and feel
metadata.seoDescription: An empathy map is a one-page snapshot of what someone says, thinks, does and feels. Learn how to make one from interviews and spot the gaps.

quiz.question: Which quadrant is the most directly observable?
quiz.why: You can see actions. Thoughts and feelings are usually inferred.

quiz.question: Someone says "no problem" but keeps frantically refreshing an app. What is that?
options: A gap between what they say and what they do
quiz.why: Gaps like this show where the real need or worry is.

quiz.question: When does an empathy map fit best?
options: After interviews, before personas or problem statements
quiz.why: It helps you make sense of what you've learned.

quiz.question: Why mark guesses with a question mark?
options: They need checking, and you should know which ones
quiz.why: Being clear about what you saw versus what you assumed keeps your research honest.

items.title: Competitor analysis
items.description: Look at what people use today, learn what works and what doesn't, and find the gap. Learn from others, don't copy them.

metadata.youllNeed: Notes app or a simple table.
metadata.seoTitle: Competitor analysis for designers: learn without copying
metadata.seoDescription: Learn how to find your real competitors, compare them on what matters to users, and spot the gap, without copying anyone.

quiz.question: A WhatsApp group where friends share timetables is a competitor to a study planner app. What kind?
quiz.why: It solves the same problem in a different way.

quiz.question: Why compare on criteria that matter to users instead of counting features?
options: More features doesn't mean a better experience for the people you serve
quiz.why: What matters is whether it works for your user's goals.

quiz.question: How should you treat app store reviews?
options: As a source of themes, aware that they come from people with strong opinions
quiz.why: They're a clue, not a complete picture.

quiz.question: What's the main goal of competitor analysis?
options: To learn what works and find a gap
quiz.why: The point is learning, not copying.

items.title: Problem statements & HMW
items.description: Turn research into one clear problem statement and a set of How Might We questions.

metadata.seoTitle: Problem statements and How Might We questions, explained
metadata.seoDescription: Turn research into one clear problem statement and a set of How Might We questions. Includes a simple template and a checklist to test yours.

quiz.question: Which is a problem statement?
options: First-year students need to know when a machine is free because they keep finding it taken
quiz.why: It names a user, a need and an insight, and it doesn't pick a solution.

quiz.question: "How might we add a free button?" is...
options: Too narrow, because it already picks a solution
quiz.why: A good HMW leaves room for different answers.

quiz.question: Where should the insight in a problem statement come from?
quiz.why: Research is what keeps the statement honest.

quiz.question: Why avoid naming a solution in your problem statement?
options: It closes off other, possibly better, ideas
quiz.why: A problem statement should open possibilities, not close them.
